title: Collaborative AI Engineering: One Dev, Two Dozen Agents, Zero Alignment — Maggie Appleton, GitHub

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 76%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk presents ACE, a GitHub Next multiplayer coding agent environment for collaborative software development where agents write code, create PRs, and operate within the IDE/PR loop.

summary: Maggie Appleton from GitHub Next's Labs team presents the case for collaborative AI engineering, challenging the 'one developer with a dozen agents' model. Software development is a team sport requiring coordination; scaling individual output doesn't solve communication problems—it worsens them. Implementation is rapidly becoming solved: code generation is fast, cheap, and improving. The new bottleneck is alignment—agreeing on what to build and why. When production is cheap, opportunity cost is the real cost. Current coordination tools (GitHub, Slack, Jira, Linear) were designed for a slower cycle with distinct planning, building, and review phases. The implementation window has collapsed to minutes between logging an issue and an agent opening a PR, eliminating traditional alignment touchpoints. Local plan modes in coding agents are unshared, and PRs bear alignment weight they weren't designed for, producing wasted work, coordination debt, and massive unreviewed PR stacks. Much alignment context lives in people's heads—business, political, product, user research—which agents cannot discover independently. She introduces ACE (Agent Collaboration Environment), a GitHub Next research prototype entering technical preview. ACE combines Slack-like multiplayer chat with coding agents and sandboxed micro VMs, each session backed by its own cloud computer on an isolated Git branch. Teammates can join sessions, see full prompting history, run terminal commands, view live previews, and prompt agents directly. PRs can be created from inside ACE with backwards-compatible links back to the session, so not everyone needs to be in ACE. Real-time multiplayer editing works in VS Code since everyone shares the same micro VM. Sessions persist—closing a laptop doesn't kill the session; teammates keep working and the agent stays always-on in the cloud. For complex features, agents write plans that teammates collaboratively edit with visible cursors, discuss, and then execute via '@Ace do this.' A dashboard summarizes unfinished work, recent PRs, and team activity, with proactive agents helping users stay oriented and aligned. Appleton closes by arguing that agents gift us time back—not to build more software faster, but to build better software through rigorous thinking, research, and alignment. In a world of fast, cheap software, quality becomes the differentiator; craftsmanship sets you apart from 'vibe-coded slop.' Doing fewer things better requires strong alignment, and agentic tools should help teams think rigorously together about hard problems.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Individual Productivity Myth
sections.summary: Maggie introduces herself and GitHub Next's Labs team ('Department of Around and Find Out'). She critiques the 'one man, two dozen Clods' model where one person with a fleet of agents replaces a team. Software is not made by one person in a vacuum—it is a team sport requiring coordination. Scaling individual output doesn't solve communication problems; it worsens them, like the 'nine women make a baby in one month' fallacy.

sections.title: Alignment as the New Bottleneck
sections.summary: Implementation is rapidly becoming a solved problem; the hard question is now 'should we build it?' When production is cheap, opportunity cost becomes the real cost. Current coordination tools (GitHub, Slack, Jira, Linear) were designed for a pre-agentic era. Agents have made the cost of team misalignment much higher, and existing tools cannot handle agentic output volumes.

sections.title: Collapsed Implementation Window and Its Consequences
sections.summary: The traditional planning, building, and review phases had multiple alignment touchpoints. The implementation window has now collapsed—time from issue to PR is minutes. Local plan modes in coding agents are unshared, and PRs carry alignment weight they weren't designed for. This produces wasted work, coordination debt, and massive unreviewed PR stacks. Most alignment context lives in people's heads, not code. Planning and building must become a continuous cycle.

sections.title: ACE Demo: Multiplayer Agent Collaboration
sections.summary: Introduction and demo of ACE (Agent Collaboration Environment) from GitHub Next, entering technical preview with a few thousand users. ACE combines Slack-like multiplayer chat with coding agents and sandboxed micro VMs on isolated Git branches. Demo shows adding color themes to a Hacker News clone, running bun commands with live preview, and teammate Nate prompting the agent directly in a shared session. ACE is designed for software development specifically, unlike Slack which lacks development primitives like diffs and terminal commands. Accessible to non-developers including designers, PMs, and customer support.

sections.title: ACE Demo Continued: PRs, Persistent Sessions, Planning, and Dashboard
sections.summary: Demo continues with creating a PR from inside ACE, backwards-compatible with GitHub, with a link back to the ACE session so not everyone needs to use ACE. Real-time multiplayer editing works in VS Code since all teammates share the same micro VM. Sessions persist—closing a laptop doesn't kill the session; teammates and agents keep working, and mobile support is coming. For complex features, agents write plans that teammates collaboratively edit with visible cursors, discuss, and execute via '@Ace do this.' A dashboard summarizes unfinished work, recent PRs, and team activity, with proactive agents helping users stay oriented. Appleton closes by arguing agents gift us time back to build better software through rigorous thinking and alignment; quality is the new differentiator, craftsmanship sets you apart from 'vibe-coded slop,' and doing fewer things better requires strong alignment. Early access expected within a couple of months.
